title: Tracking Data Applied
body: Soccer analytics with SkillCorner
Load • inspect • visualize • model
60-minute workshop | basic pandas
notes: Open with the football problem: who has a useful passing option, and what created it? Ask students to watch the same sequence before looking at model outputs.

title: Data and documentation
body: SkillCorner/opendata: match metadata, tracking, dynamic events, phases
kloppy: standardize the tracking loader
DataBallPy: metric explanations and implementation references
notes: Open the links in resources/READING_LIST.md. Tracking and derived labels are different products. The sample is Brisbane vs Perth, match 1925299; do not imply all files in the current manifest are downloaded.

title: The hour
body: 0–13: data, loading, plotting and animation
13–26: applications and physical metrics
26–50: space, graphs, passing and value
50–60: off-ball applications, interpretation and questions
notes: Timing includes notebook visits: A=7, B=4, C=5, graph=1, D=7 minutes. Slides total 31 minutes; questions 5 minutes. Avoid running full-match simulations live.

title: Coordinates are measurements
body: Frames + player identities + x/y positions + ball
Check units, pitch size, clock and attacking direction
Missing or extrapolated positions affect every downstream metric
notes: Native sample is 10 Hz. Inspect raw is_detected fields where present. Keep contiguous segments; never differentiate across a half or a gap. Dynamic-event coordinates may use different orientation from tracking.

title: Five avenues for tracking analysis
body: Events: what happened?  |  Roles: who played where?
Phases: what was the tactical context?
Physical output: how did players move?
Game modeling: which options were available and valuable?
Defense and off-ball movement connect all five
notes: Defense/off-ball movement are cross-cutting applications. Keep the core taxonomy of five avenues while making those questions visible.

title: Event detection
body: Start with possession zones and changes in ball motion
Extend to passes, receptions, runs and pressure
PathCRF: infer possession paths from player trajectories
notes: Simple proximity is a candidate detector, not ground truth. Loose balls, aerial passes and duels create ambiguity. PathCRF (2026) models dynamic graphs and possession-path inference. Validate event precision/recall with timing tolerances and hand-reviewed clips.

title: Formation, roles and phases
body: Compare shape separately in and out of possession
Normalize location before grouping players into roles
Join supplied phase intervals to frames before summarizing
notes: Shaw & Glickman show dynamic formations by game state. Mean positions alone hide role switches and transition periods. Phase definitions depend on the taxonomy. Notebook appendix demonstrates interval joins and shape summaries, not a trained formation classifier.

title: SkillCorner physical metrics
body: Volume: distance, HSR distance, sprint distance
Intensity: HSR 20–25 km/h; sprint above 25 km/h
Explosiveness: time to HSR or sprint from a qualifying start
Capacity: PSV-99 differs from absolute Peak Velocity
notes: Thresholds here refer to the documented men’s context. Use half-open bins [20,25) and [25,∞) in our teaching code to avoid overlap; this boundary convention is ours. SkillCorner describes PSV-99 over physical activities above 15 km/h; do not replace it with a percentile of all frames. Exact production smoothing and effort rules are not fully reproduced.

title: From positions to physical output
body: Clean positions → speed → speed bands → distance
Count efforts using an explicit duration and merging rule
Report valid coverage and the time denominator
notes: Distance estimate = sum(speed in m/s × dt). Our effort rule uses >=1 second and no merging. It is an educational approximation, not an exact SkillCorner count. Do not extrapolate the 15-minute sample into a full-match total or compare it directly with player-season aggregates.
cue: NOTEBOOK B · speed → efforts → distance · 4 min

title: Pitch control: three assumptions
body: Voronoi: the nearest player owns the location
Gaussian: smooth influence depends on position and motion
Arrival time: compare who can reach a location sooner
notes: Ask which model notices a player running away from the ball. Gaussian does not automatically mean calibrated probability. Our arrival-time baseline is not Spearman’s ball-aware control model.

title: Choosing a control model
body: Voronoi: fast and clear; ignores movement and contested space
Gaussian: smooth and directional; sensitive to influence parameters
Physics-based: ball/player timing; more assumptions and validation
notes: Use the same frame across panels. Our Gaussian uses a transparent illustrative covariance rather than exactly reproducing Fernández/Bornn. Control is not value: safe space behind your goal need not be valuable. Transition to pass simulation later.

title: Tracking as a graph
body: Nodes: players, with position, velocity, team and possession
Edges: relative position, distance and team relationship
A sequence becomes a dynamic graph as players move
notes: Distinguish a frame-level interaction graph from an aggregate passing network. The radius graph is an example, not a claim that only nearby players interact. Fully connected graphs can capture distant tactical relationships.

title: What a graph neural network learns
body: Messages combine a player with surrounding players
Shared updates learn interactions without depending on row order
Readouts predict a receiver, a pass outcome or a situation value
notes: Explain message passing verbally: the receiver representation changes when a defender closes the lane. Permutation-aware architectures avoid arbitrary player ordering. Temporal context needs a recurrent, temporal-attention or spatiotemporal design. Graph construction, data quality and calibration still matter.

title: Graph models in soccer
body: U.S. Soccer: counterattack success with SkillCorner tracking
DEFCON: defensive contribution through opponent EPV
TacticAI: corner receivers, shots and position suggestions
Graph attention: reception prediction and defensive influence
notes: Open the project comparison in resources/READING_LIST.md. TacticAI is a set-piece study, not a general open-play EPV model. Its task-specific code and licensed tracking data were not released. Do not interpret attention weights as causal defensive credit.

title: EPV: value the situation
body: Define the target and horizon before building the model
Estimate action selection, success and resulting value
Combine those components into expected possession value
notes: A schematic decomposition is sum over actions P(action|state) × E(value after action|state,action). Include failure/turnover branches. EPV definitions vary: expected net next-goal outcome, possession scoring probability, or fixed-horizon scoring are not interchangeable. GNNs can estimate components; EPV does not require GNNs. Fernández et al use convolutional pass surfaces.

title: Passing risk and dangerous space
body: Completion: how likely is this pass to succeed?
Accessible space: where can a pass reach teammates?
Dangerous accessible space: weight access by goal threat
notes: DAS uses physical pass simulation. The notebook calls the public accessible-space implementation and plots its actual output; it does not relabel a Gaussian map as pass completion. Ball speed assumptions, direction and offside treatment affect results. DAS is danger-weighted area, not calibrated goal probability.

title: xG and off-ball scoring opportunities
body: Tracking-informed xG adds keeper and defender context
Off-ball scoring opportunity combines access and scoring potential
Full EPV also accounts for continuation and turnover risk
notes: Use StatsBomb’s xG discussion for features and Spearman for OBSO. Never train an xG model on a handful of shots from this sample. A location-danger heuristic is not a fitted xG model.

title: Value runs that never receive the ball
body: Run threat asks what could happen if the runner were served
Space creation can benefit a different teammate
Compare changing options without claiming causal attribution
notes: SkillCorner describes run xT as the chance of a goal within 10 seconds if the run is served. Distinguish this counterfactual target from location-based event xT and observed EPV change. Supplied provider values may be explored without claiming to reproduce the model.

title: Where research goes next
body: Defense: suppress valuable passing options
Trajectory models: forecast possible team movements
Counterfactuals: evaluate alternative actions or positions
notes: DEFCON is a direct defense/EPV example. GenTac is recent preprint research: present it as emerging work, not settled operational evidence. More realistic simulated outcomes still require out-of-sample validation.

title: Validate the football answer
body: Check clips and labels before trusting metrics
Split evaluation by match; prevent nearby-frame leakage
Test calibration, model assumptions and missing-data sensitivity
Use the result to explain a football decision
notes: Close on the same sequence. Ask: which option became available, which player helped create it, and what would you need to establish that contribution reliably? Save 5 minutes for questions.
